mainTopic: Who may release vows (an expert or three laymen), and whether a husband who stays silent on purpose can still cancel his wife's vow later
overview: The amud opens by finishing two explanations of how the Torah connects the מועדי ה׳ (Festivals) to other sections. First, Festivals need קידוש בית דין because their dates depend on the court, while שבת is holy every week on its own. Second, fixing the Festivals needs a מומחה (expert), but vows can be released even by a court of הדיוטות (laymen). The גמרא challenges this from the words ״ראשי המטות״. It answers that those words teach that a single expert alone may also release vows. Then רבי חנינא rules that a husband who stays silent just to annoy his wife can still cancel her vow for up to ten days. רבא challenges him from a ברייתא about a husband who dies after staying silent. The גמרא answers that the ברייתא is about plain silence with no special intention. Finally רב חסדא begins a new challenge from a ברייתא comparing keeping and canceling a vow, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Festivals need the court to sanctify them, שבת does not
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא contrasts the מועדי ה׳, whose dates are set by the בית דין, with שבת בראשית, which is holy every week on its own.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Festivals of ה׳ need the court to sanctify them. שבת בראשית, the weekly שבת, does not need the court to sanctify it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is continuing its explanation of why the Torah places the Festivals section next to other topics. It points out that Festivals depend on the בית דין, while שבת does not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The dates of the Festivals depend on when the בית דין declares ראש חודש, so the court is part of making them holy. שבת comes every seventh day no matter what any court does. This explains why the Torah sets the Festivals apart from שבת; the next step gives a separate explanation of a different pairing, Festivals and vows.

keyTerms.meaning: Sanctification by the court (declaring the month and therefore the Festival dates)
The שבת of Creation, the weekly שבת

phrases.aramaic: מוֹעֲדֵי ה׳ צְרִיכִין קִידּוּשׁ בֵּית דִּין,
phrases.english: The Festivals of ה׳ require sanctification by the court,
Shabbat of Creation
phrases.notes: The regular weekly שבת, which goes back to the seven days of creation.

phrases.english: does not require sanctification by the court.

steps.triggerLanguage: מוֹעֲדֵי ה׳ צְרִיכִין קִידּוּשׁ בֵּית דִּין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues an explanation from earlier in the sugya about the Festivals passage
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Festivals depend on the court's sanctification, and Shabbat does not.

steps.title: Festivals need an expert, but vows can be released even by laymen
steps.stepSummary: The comparison is explained: fixing the Festivals requires a מומחה, but releasing vows does not, so even a בית דין of הדיוטות can do it.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Festivals of ה׳ need an expert. The vows section does not need an expert; even a court of laymen can release vows.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the point of the comparison between the Festivals and vows. Vows are different because they do not require an expert court.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Setting the calendar, which fixes the Festivals, can only be done by expert judges. The Torah's connection between the two topics is read as teaching a difference: releasing a vow can be done by three ordinary people. This also explains where the law that three laymen may release vows comes from.

keyTerms.meaning: An expert, a recognized qualified scholar or judge
A court made up of ordinary laymen

steps.whatToRemember: Releasing a vow does not need experts; three ordinary people are enough.

phrases.english: The Festivals of ה׳ require an expert,
but the section of vows does not require an expert,
even a court of laymen can release vows.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a separate explanation, of בן עזאי's juxtaposition of the Festivals section with the vows section, teaching who may release vows
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Vows may be released even by a court of three laymen; no expert is required.

steps.title: But the vows section mentions the heads of the tribes
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the claim that laymen may release vows, because the vows section opens with ״ראשי המטות״, the leaders.
steps.simpleTranslation: But in the vows section it is written "the heads of the tribes"!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ruling from step 2. If the Torah speaks to the leaders, how can ordinary people release vows?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase ״ראשי המטות״ sounds like vows belong to important, qualified leaders. That seems to clash with saying even הדיוטות can release them.

keyTerms.meaning: The heads of the tribes, the leaders

phrases.english: But in the section of vows
"the heads of the tribes" is written!

steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that a court of laymen can release vows
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק addresses the leaders, which suggests vows need qualified people, not laymen.

steps.title: The heads of the tribes teaches that one expert alone can release vows
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא (or רבי יוחנן) answers that ״ראשי המטות״ teaches that a single expert may release vows by himself, while three laymen can also do it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said, and some say it was רבי יוחנן: The verse is speaking about a single expert.
steps.whatsHappening: The challenge is answered. The words ״ראשי המטות״ are not a requirement for every release; they add that one expert may release a vow alone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two ways to release a vow: three laymen, or one expert by himself. The leaders mentioned in the פסוק teach the second option, so the laymen ruling stays in place.

keyTerms.meaning: And some say (it was said by someone else)

steps.whatToRemember: A vow can be released by three laymen or by one expert acting alone.
steps.confusionAlert: ״ראשי המטות״ does not mean only leaders can release vows. It adds a second way: one expert on his own.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא וְאִיתֵּימָא רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: Rav Chisda said, and some say it was Rabbi Yochanan:
It refers to a single expert.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא וְאִיתֵּימָא רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterprets the verse as adding an extra option, not setting a requirement
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The phrase about the leaders implies only qualified people may release vows
steps.terutzMaskana: The phrase teaches that one expert alone suffices; three laymen remain valid too

steps.title: A husband silent just to annoy her can still cancel for ten days
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא rules that a husband who holds back from canceling his wife's vow on purpose, to annoy her, can still cancel it even ten days later.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חנינא says: One who is silent in order to annoy her can cancel the vow even from now until ten days later.
steps.whatsHappening: A new topic begins. רבי חנינא gives a ruling about a husband's silence when he hears his wife's vow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally a husband has only the day he hears the vow to cancel it, and staying quiet counts as accepting it. רבי חנינא says that if his silence was only to make her suffer, while he planned to cancel later, his silence is not acceptance. He can still cancel even ten days later.

phrases.english: Rabbi Chanina says:
One who is silent in order to annoy her,
phrases.notes: A husband who heard his wife's vow and kept quiet on purpose to make her suffer, planning to cancel it later.

phrases.aramaic: מֵפֵר אֲפִילּוּ מִכָּאן וְעַד עֲשָׂרָה יָמִים.
phrases.english: can cancel even from now until ten days.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי חֲנִינָא הַשּׁוֹתֵק עַל מְנָת לְמֵיקַט
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic about the husband's cancellation
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Silence meant only to annoy is not acceptance of the vow, so the husband can cancel it even ten days later.

steps.title: רבא objects from a ברייתא about a husband who dies
steps.stepSummary: רבא brings a ברייתא: if the husband heard and stayed silent and died the next day, the father cannot cancel. This suggests silence past the day is final acceptance, which goes against רבי חנינא.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא raised an objection: When did they say that if the husband dies, the authority goes back to the father? When the husband did not hear, or heard and was silent, or heard and canceled and died that same day. But if he heard and accepted the vow, or heard and was silent and died the next day, the father cannot cancel.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא challenges רבי חנינא's ruling. He quotes a ברייתא about an engaged girl whose husband dies.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With an engaged girl, the father and the husband cancel her vows together. If the husband dies, his share passes back to the father. The ברייתא says that once the husband stayed silent until the next day, the vow is locked in and the father cannot cancel. It does not say "unless he was silent to annoy her," so it seems that silence past one day always counts as acceptance.

keyTerms.meaning: Raises an objection (usually from an older source)
The authority passes over to the father alone

phrases.english: Rava raised an objection:
When did they say that if the husband died
phrases.notes: This is about an engaged girl, where the father and the husband cancel her vows together.

phrases.english: the authority passes over to the father?
When the husband did not hear,
or when he heard and was silent,

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַע וְהֵפֵר וּמֵת בּוֹ בַּיּוֹם.
phrases.english: or when he heard and canceled and died on that same day.
But if he heard and confirmed it,

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַע וְשָׁתַק וּמֵת בַּיּוֹם שֶׁל אַחֲרָיו —
phrases.english: or if he heard and was silent and died on the following day,
he cannot cancel.
phrases.notes: "He" here is the father, who can no longer cancel.

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵתִיב רָבָא אֵימָתַי אָמְרוּ מֵת הַבַּעַל נִתְרוֹקְנָה רְשׁוּת לָאָב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי חנינא's ruling in step 5
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי חנינא's ruling that a husband silent to annoy can cancel for ten days
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא treats silence until the next day as final acceptance and makes no exception for silence meant to annoy.

steps.title: Isn't the ברייתא talking about silence meant to annoy?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא sharpens רבא's challenge. It suggests the ברייתא's silent husband is the one who was silent to annoy his wife.
steps.simpleTranslation: Isn't it true that the ברייתא is talking about a husband who stayed silent in order to annoy her?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא makes רבא's challenge sharper. It proposes that the ברייתא's case of 'heard and was silent' is exactly רבי חנינא's case, a husband silent to annoy.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Suppose the ברייתא includes a husband who stayed quiet to annoy his wife. Then even he loses the right to cancel once the day passes. That would directly contradict רבי חנינא, who said such a husband can cancel even ten days later.

keyTerms.meaning: Isn't it true that...? A way of offering an explanation that will cause a problem

phrases.english: What, is it not
about one who is silent in order to annoy her?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out exactly how רבא's ברייתא contradicts רבי חנינא.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי חנינא's ruling that a husband silent to annoy can cancel later
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the ברייתא's silent husband includes one silent to annoy, then his silence becomes final after the day, against רבי חנינא.

steps.title: No: the ברייתא means silence in order to keep the vow
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא is about a husband whose silence was meant to keep the vow.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is talking about a husband who stayed silent because he wanted to keep the vow.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רבי חנינא. It says the ברייתא is about a husband who stayed silent because he wanted the vow to stand.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A husband who is quiet because he wants to keep the vow has truly accepted it, so of course he cannot cancel later. That is a different case from רבי חנינא's husband, who really wants to cancel and is only teasing.

keyTerms.meaning: to keep the vow in force (to confirm it)

phrases.english: No, it is about one who is silent in order to sustain the vow.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the reading proposed in step 7 by narrowing the ברייתא to a different case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא's silent husband includes one silent to annoy.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא is about silence meant to keep the vow, so רבי חנינא is untouched.

steps.title: That case is already in the ברייתא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the answer: silence meant to keep the vow is the same as 'heard and kept it,' which the ברייתא already lists.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, that is the same as the ברייתא's earlier case of 'he heard and kept the vow'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the answer from step 8. A husband who is silent in order to keep the vow is no different from one who openly kept it, and the ברייתא already mentioned that case separately.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A ברייתא would not list the same case twice. 'Heard and was silent' must therefore mean something other than 'heard and kept it,' so the answer from step 8 fails.

phrases.english: If so,
this is the same as 'or he heard and ratified'!
phrases.notes: 'Or he heard and ratified' is a separate case listed earlier in the same ברייתא that רבא quoted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer from step 8 because it would make a phrase in the ברייתא repeat itself.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that the ברייתא means silence meant to keep the vow
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: That case is identical to 'heard and ratified,' already in the ברייתא, so it would be listed twice.

steps.title: Rather, the ברייתא means plain silence
steps.stepSummary: The final answer: the ברייתא is about a husband who was silent with no special intention.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is talking about a husband who was just silent, with no particular intention.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a new answer. The ברייתא's case is ordinary silence with no specific intention, which is different from רבי חנינא's case of silence meant to annoy.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Plain silence through the day counts as accepting the vow, so cancelling afterward does not work. A husband silent to annoy shows that he really plans to cancel, so רבי חנינא's ruling still holds.
steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא is about plain silence, which becomes final when the day ends. רבי חנינא's case is silence meant to annoy, which does not count as acceptance. So רבי חנינא stands.

phrases.english: Rather, it is about one who is silent without any specific intent.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the failed answer from step 8 with a new reading that keeps all of the ברייתא's cases separate.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא's silence was either meant to annoy or meant to keep the vow.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא is about plain silence, so רבי חנינא's case of silence meant to annoy is not covered.

steps.title: רב חסדא begins a new challenge
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא opens a new objection to רבי חנינא from a ברייתא comparing keeping a vow and canceling it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא raised an objection: keeping a vow is stricter than canceling in one way, and canceling is stricter than keeping in another. The way keeping is stricter is...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a new challenge. רב חסדא starts quoting a ברייתא that compares keeping (הקם) and canceling (הפר) a vow, and the quote continues past this point.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא says each action has its own strictness. The details of the strictness of keeping a vow come next, and רב חסדא will use them to challenge רבי חנינא.

keyTerms.meaning: raises an objection from a source

phrases.english: Rav Ḥisda raised an objection:
There is a stringency in ratification over nullification,
and in nullification over ratification.
The stringency in ratification is —

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After רבא's challenge was answered, a second objection to רבי חנינא begins from a different ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי חנינא's ruling about a husband silent to annoy
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The attack begins here but is not finished. The ברייתא's comparison of keeping and canceling a vow will be used against רבי חנינא.
